A Clinical Introduction to Lacanian Psychoanalysis: Therory and Technique. Bruce Fink. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1997. 220. pp

William Hurst

William Hurst

William Hurst  

As a long time student of Lacanian thought, I consider this exploration of its clinical dimensions to be extraordinary good. Fink presents Lacan's ideas in the context for which they were intended, and he renderes them readily accessible, even to those who have no previous acquaintance with Lacan. At the same time, Fink succeeds admirably, even when the oversimplifies, in preserving the polyvalent and allusional character of Lacanian thought.

A reader of this book might well find herself or himself in a position like that of the young Marx, after he read Hegel's Phenomenology of Spirit. Marx had become an Hegelian. One cannot read Hegel and understand him without having one's ways of thinking changed in some way. Lacan may have wished that his readers would be similarly affected. Like Hegel, he made the task of understanding him difficult, writing in a dense and, some would contend, impenetrable prose. Yet, for the reader who could find his or her way in, there was no easy way out. One would find oneself, of necessity, adopting the notions and patterns of thought that had constructed that prose. Lacan, however unlike. Hegel, did not really intend his writings simply to be read (p. xii).

The group setting gains much of its therapeutic leverage from the fact that it requires its members to experience and process feelings and impulses arising from a multiplicity of stimuli, but as Rosenthal and Bernstein (1999) point out in their papers, inevitably heightens the vulnerability of patients to narcissistic injury. Goldberg (1999) favors placing her patients into group after two years of individual analysis so that they will experience primitive levels of regression. This theoretical divide is explored. Rosenthal takes up the analyst's narcissistic vulnerability in the group setting. The author discusses how the analyst's heightened emotional vulnerability can either contribute to or deter therapeutic progress. The author ends with a discussion of Marshall's (1999) approach to group supervision and a supervisory interaction he once had with Spotnitz.

Leslie Rosenthal   Founder and Dean of Group Studies at the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies. He has served as group therapy consultant to a wide variety of social agencies, hospitals, and educational institutes. He is author of Resolving Resistance in Group Psychotherapy and numerous papers on psychoanalytic group psychotherapy.

Protecting the individual from the destructive effects of emotional over-stimulation has been a historic concern of modern psychoanalysis. That effect is heightened within the group setting. The highly charged atmosphere of the group is seen as deriving from the exposure of each member to his or her feelings toward all the occupants of the meeting room and all of their verbal and nonverbal responses to him or her. The individual's capacity to assimilate this volatile mixture requires careful study and evaluation. This paper focuses on the crucial role of the group therapist in monitoring and regulating the degree of emotional excitation to which individuals and group are exposed. The varied sources of overstimulation are identified. Consideration is given to the impact on the group therapist of his exposure to transferences of all the members and to his own subjective and induced feelings. It is noted that the emotional bombardment to which the therapist is subject is fertile ground for the development of overt and covert counterresistances.

This volume, containing twenty remarkable papers from psychoanalysts and child therapists around the world, is a fitting homage to the independent-minded, straight-talking woman who devoted her career to penetrating and understanding the inner world of autistic children. Contributors include students, colleagues, collaborators, supervisees, and friends, who add rich case material and considered theoretical review and extension to revealing memoirs of Frances Tustin herself.

Born in 1913 in England, Tustin came to study at the Tavistock Clinic to become a child psychotherapist. Under the tutelage of Esther Bick, founder of Kleinian infant observation, she also studied with John Bowlby, who originated attachment and bonding theory, and began a 14-year personal analysis with Wilfred Bion.

The authors recount limitations of their early experiences as teachers without the benefits of the modern analytic group understanding of countertransference and without the applications of the concept of the class as a group. They describe how developments in the fields of education and modern psychoanalysis stimulated developments in their own awareness of the significance and usefulness of countertransference experiences for the teacher-educator as for the modern analytic group leader, and enriched their experience of teaching. A review of the literature in education and modern psychoanalysis on the subject of countertransference is summarized and anecdotes are given.

This is a splendid book. It is an edited collection of eighteen papers in addition to a well-written introduction by Roy Schafer that discusses some of the important Kleinian concepts like paranoid-schizoid and depressive positions, transference, countertransference, projective identification, containment, and enactment. The papers are among some of the finest contributions of the British Kleinian analysts like Robin Anderson, Ronald Britton, Eric Brenman, Michael Feldman, Betty Joseph, Edna O'Shaughnessy, Irma Brenman Pick, Ruth Riesenberg-Malcolm, Hanna Segal, Elizabeth Spillus, Ignes Sodre and John Steiner. The papers covers a wide range of important theoretical and clinical issues that are all the focus of contemporary psychoanalysis. The editor introduces every paper with a brief but rich commentary which facilitates the grasp of the central themes of the papers.

All the papers that constitute this volume manifest an intellectual and emotional openness to different conceptual schemes and clinical tools. There is a solid awareness of the relationship between theory and observation. Some of the writers explicitly warn the reader against the intellectual imposition of his or her favorite theoretical constructs on clinical materials. They remind us that overworking a theory often leads to psychoanalytic fabrications and pseudounderstanding. Discussions in all the papers aim to capture the genuine experience of the analytic hour. All writers are attuned to the moment to moment shifts in the transference-countertransference nuances of the analytic encounter.

The question of the importance of the analytic relationship begins with a discussion of clinical facts. In the first paper Edna O'Shaughnessy examines the notion of scientific clinical facts by placing it within the context of theory, method, and language. Borrowing an expression from Thomas Nagle, she argues that clinical facts represent a partial view from somewhere. She points out that clutching at “objectivity” certainly is at times a defense against the anxiety of not knowing. She makes a distinction between facts and clinical facts. There are many facts about the patient's personality, mental life, internalized history of object relationships, etc. However, they become clinical facts only when they come to reflect the immediate emotional reality of the session. And that includes the lived facts of the shifting object relations between the patient and the analyst. O'Shaughnessy reminds the reader that the identification of these facts is not based on observation and inference from “basic data.

Divided into two sections, the major one on clinical psychoanalysis and the other on literature and politics, the book is a collection of wonderful articles written over a period of twenty years. All have been revised for this collection, and all of them could be useful reading for clinicians who work with preoedipal patients.

Segal, pioneer of the “British” school, follower and interpreter of Melanie Klein, is also recognized as a respected psychoanalyst in her own right. She has been most interested in working with those patients considered narcissistic and/or emotionally regressed to infantile levels. As Steiner points out, Hanna Segal's writing ably elaborates two inter-related themes: the “clinical usefulness of the concept of the death instinct” and of the “relationship between phantasy and reality.” These themes are given very original treatment in the book and point us toward an understanding of many other ideas put forth by Segal herself and other members of the “British” school, such as projective identification, depressive position, paranoid-schizoid position, ideal objects, and persecutors.

Although this reviewer believes that the entire book is well worth reading, two of the articles stand out as major contributions to psychoanalytic literature.

Marge Blaine   Psychoanalyst in private practice in Brooklyn and New York City. She graduated from the Union Institute, the Center for the Advancement of Group Studies, and Mid-Manhattan Institute. She currently teaches at mid-Manhattan and the New School University. She was the recepient of a 1998 Gradiva Award from the National Association for the Advancement of Psychoanalysis for an earlier version of the paper published here.

Mounting evidence indicates that old age provides opportunities for further growth. This paper explores the effects of modern psychoanalytic techniques on emotional communication in a group of well-functioning older adults over a period of four years. It examines the results of working with resistances manifested in individuals and the group, and demonstrates how individuals and the group itself changed and grew. Working with resistance from a modern psychoanalytic perspective is detailed, and the historical background of therapy for elders is described. Clinical vignettes illustrate the changes that occurred and demonstrate how the lives of group members were enhanced through participation in this group experience.

Elaine Hurst

Elaine Hurst

Elaine Hurst  

It has often been the case that philosophers and psychoanalysts—despite their manifestly common interest in understanding the nature and vicissitudes of the human mind—look warily upon the approaches taken by one another's discipline. Psychoanalysts tend to chide philosophers for their intellectual aridity, while philosophers often cite psychoanalysts for conceptual obscurity or logical imprecision. In this rich, thought-provoking book, Jonathan Lear—himself both a philosopher and a practicing psychoanalyst—bridges the chasm of division with ease and grace.

The book is aptly named. It demonstrates the value of being “open minded” (in the sense of being receptive to what the varied approaches have to offer), while it elucidates our understanding of the human psyche (it investigates the mind, “opening it up” for study) in a manner which sacrifices neither emotional depth nor intellectual rigor.

In this collection of essays, several of which have been previously published—including Lear's popular New Republic piece in defense of psychoanalysis, “The Shrink Is In,” as well as other articles which originally appeared in academic journals or anthologies—Lear engages the reader in an exploration which is, at times, disarmingly simple, yet profoundly evocative of both thought and feeling.

Arnold Bernstein   Certified psychologist and a psychoanalyst in private practice in New York City. He is a training analyst, supervisor, and Dean of Professional Programs at the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies and Professor Emeritus in Psychology at Queens College of the City University of New York. He is also a training and control analyst at the National Psychological Association for Psychoanalysis and an adjunct professor at the Union for Experimenting Colleges and Universities.

The thesis is offered that not only is the resistance to entering therapy groups a result of narcissism, but that all resistance might have their root in narcissism, ultimately including even the resistance to dying. Resistance and narcissism are related to power and love, derivatives of Thanatos and Eros.

Narcissism can be one's best friend or one's worst enemy, depending upon whether it functions in the service of self-preservation or self-destruction. It is destructive to therapeutic group when it conflicts with Eros, the love of otehrs. In Freud's words, group are held together by libidinal ties. The healing power of a therapy group resides in these ties, not in the leader, but in the processing of all the emotional and verbal encounters that transpire within the group.

The ability to make at least fleeting identifications with others is vital to healthy interpersonal functioning. Group treatment is the ideal venue in which to develop this ability. The author studied the analytic sessions of a pregnant patient just before and after she gave birth. The session material demonstrated that Winnicott's concept of primary maternal preoccupation accurately describes the emotional experience of both the patient and the analyst. She is a faculty member, training analyst, and supervisor at both institutes and practices in New York City and Boston. Why does analysis take so long? Destructive urges associated with the death instinct and the repetition compulsion give a conceptual framework for the existence of time-wasting in analysis. Constructive ends may also be served by repetition. Repetition may offer pleasure, mastery, and the conservation of needed relationships, including the maintenance of a long-term relationship with analyst. Modern analysis has developed some specific theories and the techniques which have relevance to this issue. The anaclitic relationship is an example of a favorable outcome of the ability to spend a lot of time before mutative change takes place.

Phyllis Meadow

Phyllis Meadow

Brookline, MA 02146

Phyllis Meadow  

The paper traces the author's evolution as a group analyst from the early 1950s to the present. It explores narcissism and the narcissistic transference as manifested in groups, induction and its use as emotional communication to resolve narcissistic resistances in groups, and the role of drive theory in her method of working with groups. Two case vignettes are presented to illustrate the concepts. The first involves an individual's treatment-destructive resistance and the other a group of males who work through the emptiness of narcissism and the desperation of action to realize their unfulfilled longings for love and relatedness.

Primitive Mental States: Across the Lifespan. Shelly Alhanati and Katina Kostoulas, eds. Northvale, NJ: Jason Aronson, 1997. 260 pp.

William Hurst

William Hurst

William Hurst  

This is quite a good book, with a focus on many varied senses of the “primitive,” and with many potential rewards for the modern psychoanalytic reader. While Bion, Klein, and their followers are particularly significant presences in this work, attention is given to other points of view as well, including the Kohutian and the object rationalist. As the first volume in a projected series devoted to the study of primitive mental states, this book represents a significant first step and deserves a serious reading. It represents also the theoretical, clinical, and educational commitments of the Psychoanalytic Center of California, which has endorsed the project, although it assumes no administrative responsibility for it. The principal editors and a fair number of the authors in this volume are either members of that institute or are in some way related to it, and the study itself evidently embodies its eclectic orientation. The overall philosophy of the Psychoanalytic Center of California resembes in several ways that of modern psychoanalytic institutes.
